preamble.summary: Judith is given a place in Holofernes' camp. She establishes a routine of going out each night to pray and bathe in the valley spring — a pattern that will provide her escape route. She eats only her own provisions, maintaining ritual purity. Three days pass as she settles into camp life, gaining trust and freedom of movement.
preamble.remarkable: The Vulgate chapter 11 is significantly condensed compared to the Greek text. Jerome's version focuses on Judith's daily routine of nocturnal prayer and ritual bathing, establishing the practical logistics that make her escape possible. Every spiritual discipline doubles as tactical preparation.
preamble.friction: Judith's maintained ritual purity in enemy territory creates an implicit contrast: she lives among pagans but remains consecrated, a walking holy space amid defilement.
preamble.connections: Her nightly excursions to pray echo Daniel's habit of thrice-daily prayer toward Jerusalem (Daniel 6:10). The ritual bathing connects to prophetic and priestly purification traditions.

verses.text_latin: Tunc iussit eam introire ubi repositi erant thesauri eius et iussit illic manere eam et constituit quid daretur illi de convivio suo.
verses.rendering: Then he commanded her to enter where his treasures were stored, and ordered her to remain there, and appointed what should be given to her from his own table.

verses.text_latin: Cui respondit Iudith et dixit nunc manducare non potero ex his quae mihi praecipis tribui ne veniat super me offensio sed de his quae mecum detuli manducabo.
verses.rendering: Judith answered and said: I cannot now eat from those things you command to be given me, lest an offense come upon me. But I will eat from what I have brought with me.
translator_notes: Maintaining kosher dietary laws in enemy territory — a direct parallel to Daniel 1:8.

key_terms.rendered_as: lest an offense come upon me
key_terms.note: Offensio here means ritual defilement — she frames her kosher observance in terms a pagan might respect as religious scruple.

verses.text_latin: Cui Holofernes dixit si defecerint tibi ista quae tecum detulisti quid faciemus tibi dare similia.
verses.rendering: Holofernes said to her: If these things you have brought with you run out, what shall we do to provide you the same?

verses.text_latin: Et dixit Iudith vivit anima tua domine mi quoniam non expendet omnia haec ancilla tua donec faciat Deus in manu mea haec quae cogitavi.
verses.rendering: Judith said: As your soul lives, my lord, your handmaid shall not use up all these things before God accomplishes by my hand what I have planned.
translator_notes: Another masterpiece of double meaning: 'what I have planned' — Holofernes hears a promise of Israel's betrayal; the reader knows it means his death.

verses.text_latin: Et induxerunt illam servi eius in tabernaculum quod praeceperat.
verses.rendering: His servants led her into the tent he had appointed.

verses.text_latin: Et petiit dum introiret ut daretur sibi copia nocte et ante lucem egrediendi foras ad orationem et deprecandi Dominum.
verses.rendering: As she entered, she requested that she be given freedom to go out at night and before dawn for prayer, to beseech the Lord.
translator_notes: This is the critical logistical request — establishing her pattern of nocturnal movement that will enable her escape with Holofernes' head.

verses.text_latin: Et praecepit cubiculariis suis ut sicut placeret illi exiret et introiret ad adorandum Deum suum per triduum.
verses.rendering: He commanded his attendants that she might come and go as she pleased to worship her God for three days.

verses.text_latin: Et exiebat noctibus in vallem Bethuliae et baptizabat se in fonte aquae.
verses.rendering: She went out each night into the valley of Bethulia and bathed herself in the spring of water.

key_terms.note: Baptizare here means ritual immersion — a purification rite, not mere hygiene. The spring the Assyrians thought they controlled still serves God's agent.

verses.text_latin: Et ut ascendebat orabat Dominum Deum Israhel ut dirigeret viam eius ad liberationem populi sui.
verses.rendering: And as she came up from the water, she prayed to the Lord God of Israel to direct her way for the deliverance of his people.

verses.text_latin: Et introiens munda manebat in tabernaculo quousque acciperet escam suam in vespera.
verses.rendering: Entering ritually clean, she remained in the tent until she received her food in the evening.

key_terms.note: Her purity is maintained through immersion — she enters the pagan space in a state of holiness.

verses.text_latin: Et factum est in quarto die Holofernes fecit cenam servis suis et dixit ad Vagao eunuchum suum vade et suade Hebraeam illam ut sponte consentiat habitare mecum.
verses.rendering: On the fourth day, Holofernes made a feast for his servants and said to Bagoas his eunuch: Go and persuade that Hebrew woman to consent willingly to dwell with me.
translator_notes: The name Bagoas (Vagao) is historically attested as a Persian eunuch name. The invitation to 'dwell with him' is transparently sexual.

key_terms.note: The eunuch as go-between for a sexual proposition — a stock figure in ancient Near Eastern court narratives.

verses.text_latin: Foedissimum enim apud Assyrios est si femina inrideat virum agendo ut immunis ab eo transeat.
verses.rendering: For among the Assyrians it is considered most shameful if a woman should mock a man by acting so as to pass from him untouched.

verses.text_latin: Tunc introivit Vagao ad Iudith et dixit non vereatur bona puella introire ad dominum meum ut honorificetur ante faciem eius ut manducet cum eo et bibat vinum in iucunditate.
verses.rendering: Then Bagoas went in to Judith and said: Let the good young woman not hesitate to come in to my lord, to be honored before his face, to eat with him and drink wine in gladness.

verses.text_latin: Cui Iudith respondit quae sum ego ut contradicam domino meo.
verses.rendering: Judith answered him: Who am I to refuse my lord?
translator_notes: Apparent submission that conceals lethal intent. The question 'Who am I to refuse my lord?' reads as modesty to Bagoas and as ironic resignation to the reader.

verses.text_latin: Omne quod erit ante oculos eius bonum et optimum faciam quidquid autem illi placuerit hoc mihi erit optimum omnibus diebus vitae meae.
verses.rendering: Whatever is good and best before his eyes, I will do. And whatever pleases him — that shall be best for me all the days of my life.

verses.text_latin: Et surrexit et ornavit se vestimento suo et ingressa stetit ante faciem eius.
verses.rendering: She rose, adorned herself in her finest garments, and entering, stood before his face.

verses.text_latin: Cor autem Holofernis concussum est erat enim ardens in concupiscentia eius.
verses.rendering: The heart of Holofernes was shaken, for he burned with desire for her.

key_terms.note: The snare of his eyes that Judith prayed for (9:13) has sprung. His lust is his undoing.

verses.text_latin: Dixitque ad eam Holofernes bibe nunc et adcumbe in iucunditate quoniam invenisti gratiam coram me.
verses.rendering: Holofernes said to her: Drink now and recline in gladness, for you have found favor before me.

verses.text_latin: Et dixit Iudith bibam domine quoniam magnificata est anima mea hodie prae omnibus diebus meis.
verses.rendering: Judith said: I will drink, my lord, for my soul is magnified today beyond all my days.
translator_notes: 'Magnificata est anima mea' — 'my soul is magnified' — echoes the Magnificat opening (Luke 1:46). The verbal parallel between Judith and Mary is ancient and deliberate in liturgical tradition.

key_terms.note: The Magnificat echo — Judith prefigures Mary in Catholic and Orthodox typology.

verses.text_latin: Et accepit et manducavit et bibit coram ipso ea quae paraverat illi ancilla eius.
verses.rendering: She took and ate and drank before him what her maidservant had prepared for her.
translator_notes: She eats her own kosher food, not his — maintaining ritual purity even at his banquet table.

verses.text_latin: Et iucundus factus est Holofernes ad eam bibitque vinum nimis multum quantum numquam biberat in vita sua.
verses.rendering: Holofernes was delighted with her and drank an exceedingly great quantity of wine — more than he had ever drunk in his life.
translator_notes: The climactic detail: Holofernes drinks himself into a stupor. His indulgence — the vice of the undisciplined — creates the opening for the disciplined woman's strike.

key_terms.latin: vinum nimis multum quantum numquam biberat in vita sua
key_terms.rendered_as: an exceedingly great quantity of wine — more than he had ever drunk in his life
key_terms.note: His greatest indulgence becomes his death sentence. The irony is absolute.
